lines.title: This is a closer look at how Semantic Router dot net decides where each prompt goes, and what happens when something goes wrong.
lines.two-questions: Every request gets two questions. First, what does this prompt actually need? That's a tier, plus capabilities like code or tools. And second, which of your models is the cheapest one that can deliver it?
lines.routes: The first answer comes from routes. A route is a handful of example prompts, with the tier that kind of request needs. The starter config has eight of them, from small talk at the bottom, to debugging and agentic coding at the top.
lines.tester: When a prompt comes in, the router embeds it and compares it with every example. This one is closest to complex code, at point eight seven. So it needs tier four, and a model that can code.
lines.simple: Now a small task: a regex for email addresses. That's simple code, so tier two is plenty, and the local coder ranks first.
lines.complex: Ask for the same regex, but with a list of things to reason through, and the complexity score climbs. Length, code, structure, and words like step by step all count. Above zero point six five, the prompt moves up a tier.
lines.tiers: Every model sits on a tier too. The tiers page lines them up: which routes need each tier, and which models can serve it. A tier with nothing to serve it shows up in red.
lines.strategy: Then a strategy ranks the models that qualify. The default is cheapest capable. Local models and your subscription both cost nothing, so the lowest tier that's good enough wins. Switch to auto best, and the same prompt goes straight to the most capable model.
lines.agents: Coding agents send more than prompts. Every Claude Code turn carries its tools, so only models that can call tools are candidates.
lines.toolloop: Here, the local model asks to read the read me. Claude Code runs the tool, and sends the result back. The router keeps that result with the model that asked for it, so a single turn never gets split across two models.
lines.callout: You can always take over, too. Start a message with at opus, at local, or at tier two, and the router does exactly that.
lines.privacy: Some data should never leave your machine. With secret detection on, a conversation that contains a credential stays local from then on. Even after you've asked for Opus.
lines.failover: And when a model is down, or out of quota, it cools down and the next one takes over. The endpoints table shows what's cooling down, and until when.
lines.activity: Every decision explains itself. The activity log shows the route, the score, the tier, and every model a request tried.
lines.evaluate: And the evaluate page runs a labelled set of prompts through your configuration. So you know how often the router gets it right, and exactly which prompts it gets wrong, before you change anything.
lines.end: That's how a prompt gets routed. Next time, we'll tune all of this for your own models. Semantic Router dot net is open source, and MIT licensed.
